introduction: Madame Tussauds Budapest is a recent attraction in an older building: a wax-figure exhibition that opened in 2023 inside the Palazzo Dorottya, a Pest house that stood empty for almost a decade before its renovation.
chapters: From London waxworks to a global brand

The name comes from Anna Marie Tussaud (1761-1850), a French artist who specialised in life-size figures of famous people. According to a Budapest Times report, the first Madame Tussauds exhibition opened in London in 1835. That idea, a gallery of recognisable personalities modelled in wax, is the one the Budapest attraction continues, with figures chosen after market research and negotiations over the right to portray each person.
A house on Dorottya utca

The exhibition is in the Palazzo Dorottya at Dorottya utca 6, in Pest beside Vörösmarty Square. Hungarian architectural press knows the building as the former Wurm House and refers to it as the Pollack-Hauszmann building. Before its renovation it was unoccupied for almost a decade. The project was commissioned by RDM, a group of Italian investors, and led by the Zoboki Demeter and Partners architectural office, with a facade refresh and restoration of the building's original look. Afterwards the lower storeys held a garage and commercial spaces and the upper floors offices and residential units.
Opening in 2023

Madame Tussauds Budapest opened on 25 May 2023, filling about 2,000 square metres of the palazzo. Reports on the opening describe a red carpet route past around fifty figures. We Love Budapest reported that each figure was made by about twenty artists at a workshop near London, taking three to four months, and that Hungarian craftspeople, including stained-glass artists, architectural sculptors, woodcarvers and set designers, made the settings. Press coverage also noted that organisers asked the public which personalities they most wanted to see.

introduction: The Light Art Museum occupies a market hall from the 1890s. Its story runs from a working food market through a renovation, a pandemic closure and a 2022 conversion to a museum of light, with a temporary closure announced for mid-2026.
chapters: A market hall for central Pest

The hall at Hold utca 13 was built between 1892 and 1896 to plans by the architect Győző Czigler as Market Hall No. 5, one of six large market halls built in Budapest in the Austro-Hungarian era. Hungarian Wikipedia describes it as eclectic, covering 2,107 square metres, with 190 permanent and 80 temporary stalls, plus police and ambulance rooms, a coffee-measuring point and a market supervision office. A restaurant and a meat-inspection building were attached.
Renovation, renaming and closure

The hall was renovated in 2014 and renamed Belvárosi Piac, the Inner City Market, and gradually became a producers' market. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, declining tourism during the COVID-19 pandemic led to a temporary closure from 1 January 2021. A local article on the museum recalls that the hall had once been a place where people bought produce, fish and meat, and that this activity had ended.
From market to museum of light

The building reopened to visitors in September 2022 as the Light Art Museum Budapest, according to We Love Budapest and a sponsored report; Hungarian Wikipedia gives both summer 2022 and November 2022, so the exact start is unclear. An opening show, The Revolution of Light, featured work by György Kepes, László Moholy-Nagy and Victor Vasarely alongside contemporary Hungarian-origin artists, and was extended to 15 August 2023. A June 2026 article reported that the museum would temporarily close at the end of June 2026 and gave no reopening date, so check the official site for its current status.

introduction: Cinema Mystica began as a 2022 exhibition on Margaret Island and moved in 2023 to its present home in the Párisi Udvar, a Pest arcade that was restored and reopened as a hotel building in 2019.
chapters: A first showing on Margaret Island

A May 2022 We Love Budapest article describes the first Cinema Mystica exhibition at Kristály Színtér, a cultural centre on Margaret Island, in a Bauhaus-style building that the article says was formerly a mineral water-bottling plant. It showed sixteen new-media installations that combined art and technology, including Let There Be Life, a room with video projected on the walls, ceiling and floor showing the origin of life. The article names the visual artist and musician Dávid Vígh (Takkra) and the visual group Glowing Bulbs among those involved, and does not identify the founders of Cinema Mystica.
The Párisi Udvar

The permanent home is in the Párisi Udvar at Ferenciek tere 10. According to We Love Budapest, the Downtown Savings Bank commissioned the architect Henry Schmahl, who conceived the building in 1912-1913, and it was one of Budapest's earliest reinforced concrete buildings. It became a historic monument in 1976 and emptied out for years after popular shops such as the Jégbüfé ice-cream parlour and a hologram shop moved out. Restoration began in 2014, and the building reopened as a hotel in The Unbound Collection by Hyatt, with the passage open to the public.
A permanent immersive venue

In July 2023 We Love Budapest reported that Cinema Mystica had moved into the Párisi Udvar as the country's first permanent immersive digital exhibition space, with 21 installations in ten rooms, 85 projectors and five kilometres of cable. By July 2026, the venue marked its third anniversary, reporting more than 500,000 visitors and four exhibitions so far. The current show, Form in Flux, has run since early summer 2025 with works by 26 Hungarian and international artists.

introduction: IKONO Budapest is the Hungarian branch of a young European network of immersive art museums. Its short history runs from a first venue in Madrid in 2020 to a Váci utca opening in September 2023.
chapters: From Madrid to a European network

According to We Love Budapest, the IKONO brand first opened in Madrid in 2020 and then expanded to Rome, Barcelona, Vienna, Copenhagen and Berlin. A September 2023 article said the first IKONO exhibit had opened in Madrid about three years earlier, with Rome and Barcelona following before Budapest. The official IKONO site presents Budapest as part of the IKONO Xperience network, which also has locations in Madrid, Barcelona, Vienna, Copenhagen and Berlin. The sources consulted do not name the founders.
Arriving on Váci utca in 2023

The Budapest venue is at Váci utca 27, on the pedestrian shopping street of downtown Pest, and has been open since September 2023. A We Love Budapest article published on 5 September 2023 described it as recently opened, with ten fantasy worlds including a colourful jungle, a large ball pool, a UV-painted sea installation, a light-painting room inspired by Picasso's experiments with light and a quiet room. Sources give no details about the building's earlier history.
Rooms and collaborating artists

The rooms were created with international artists. The opening article names Koketit, Heather Bellino and Kimberly Leahey, and the venue profile says the Budapest venue was created with the American visual artist Heather Bellino. The official site now describes twelve rooms, naming experiences such as the Lantern Sanctuary, light painting and The Love Within, an immersive work by Koketit about self-love, so the programme has been extended since opening or is counted differently.

introduction: Tropicarium grew out of a concept first built in Sweden in 1990 and opened in Budapest on 26 May 2000, inside the Campona Shopping Center, after eight months of construction.
chapters: An idea from Sweden

A history page for the attraction credits the concept to Károly Farkasdi, a Hungarian businessman who lived in Sweden between 1963 and 1998. In 1990 he and his family created the first such establishment in Kolmården, Sweden. The Budapest aquarium is a separate venue from the Swedish one.
Building at Campona, 1999-2000

Intensive construction began in Budapest in September 1999 and took eight months. A visitor guide says the work involved hundreds of tons of concrete and iron, filtration, purification and IT systems, and that most of the decoration was handcrafted by Tropicarium staff. The facility opened on 26 May 2000 in the Campona Shopping Center, on the outskirts of the city, and was described as the largest sea aquarium in Central Europe at almost 3,000 square metres, arranged in eight rooms.
Growing after opening

The history page says the operators add one or two new aquariums or terrariums at a time to give returning visitors something new. About eight years after the opening, they reported nearly four million visitors. That page was last updated in 2010, so later developments are not covered there. Check the official site for the present exhibits, which include sand tiger and brown reef sharks and a 12-metre viewing tunnel.
